title: How Do You Handle the Fast Evolution of AI?
author: Midnight-Magistrate
selftext:
I’m currently developing a game and using AI-generated graphics. Initially, I created the images using SDXL, but now I’m in the process of refining or recreating them with FLUX. Since I’m still in the early stages of development, this is manageable, but as the project progresses and I have hundreds of images, this approach won’t be sustainable.

The issue is that FLUX produces a slightly different style compared to the models and LoRAs I used with SDXL. With the rapid development of AI tools and generative art, even more advanced models are bound to emerge in the future.

How do you handle this constant evolution of AI tools? Do you stick with one tool for consistency or adapt to the latest advancements as they come? Would love to hear your thoughts!

comments.author: Thomas-Lore
comments.body:
I am trying to speed up the process from concept to release, so the depreciation of tools used is not that visible. For example my small game Entangled on itch -  https://magory.itch.io/entangled - took only around 120 hours to make (not counting thinking out the story, I do that walking in the forest and consider that enjoying my free time).

Another thing is making sure the style chosen for a specific game does not show any limitations of the current models - so it does not start to look dated before the game is even released. (Entangled is not a good example of that, I think it could have lookes better, there are many shortcuts I had to take graphically with it.)

replies.author: Midnight-Magistrate
replies.body: Your game looks really nice and is right up my alley. Wishlisted you upcoming game on Steam too!

comments.author: _stevencasteel_
comments.body:
I thought I was gonna write a book a month when I started using GPT 3.0.

It took me over a year. The audiobook took 5 months.

Whatever this next GPT-5 level tech is that comes out next year will be able to make something much higher quality than what I toiled over probably a staggeringly quick amount of time.

Increase your scope as increased scope gets cheaper / easier.

What I keep hearing from game devs ('cause their advice applies to all entrepreneurs in many ways) is to fail fast / succeed fast.

Publish small projects quickly.

Why spend 5 years working on something that will be able to be made with AI agents in a couple weeks 5 years from now?

comments.author: fisj
comments.body:
I see this as the same question as developing a game around features in an engine. Unreal 5 has many features where they're iterating at a furious pace, Control Rigs, Chaos Physics, State Trees, Motion Matching. It really comes down to building a pipeline, locking it down for production and using it - without moving onto the next shiny version.

Secondly, you can build workflows where upgrading AI models won't be \_that\_ painful. Save your prompts and seeds, use the API to iterate on content, or use nodes like ipadapter so you're not dependent so heavily on a seed. Lean more heavily on controlnets where you reliably get precisely what you want. Its more work, but you can future proof things by pipelining and making sure you can automate regeneration of content rapidly.

comments.author: Audiogus
comments.body: I have been sticking with SDXL, specifically Crystal Clear Prime and Brixl.  One is more loosey goosey and creative while the other is more grounded and 3D feeling.  I use img2img / control net back and forth between the two of them.  I can draw / paint / 3D model which helps as far as consistency but more than anything I make sure not to bite off more than I can chew when just roughing things out and planning.  I need to get this stuff in engine in 3D and not looking like AI so I am the bottleneck in the end.

comments.author: Square_Tooth_1816
comments.body: how is your game going? do you feel like ai helped your efforts?

replies.author: Midnight-Magistrate
replies.body: The game shipped in August 2024. AI-generated art was part of the release and the visuals got explicit praise from reviewers. Beyond the art, using AI for coding, structuring our ideas, and the publishing process has become a core part of how we work. For a two-person team, it's been the right fit. We're applying the same workflow to the next project we're currently working on.
